title: Spell Damage Without Near Neighbours
statement:
A wizard owns a set of spells. power[i] is the damage of spell i, and several spells may have the same damage. Each spell can be cast at most once.

The spells interfere: if the wizard casts any spell with damage d, he can cast no spell whose damage is d − 2, d − 1, d + 1 or d + 2. Spells with exactly the same damage do not interfere with each other.

Return the largest total damage he can deal.

examples.why: Cast both 2s and the 6. The 3 is too close to the 2s, and the 5 is too close to the 6.
Chosen damages must be at least 3 apart. The best such set is 5 and 8.
Grabbing the biggest spell first takes 10, then 7, for 17. Casting both 9s alone gives 18.

hints: Equal damages never conflict, so if you cast one spell with damage d, you may as well cast all of them. Group by value.
Sort the distinct values. Now it looks like robbing houses on a street: taking value v forbids its close neighbours. Let best[i] be the answer using only the first i distinct values.
best[i] = max(best[i − 1], total[i] + best[j]), where j is the last distinct value smaller than v[i] − 2. A pointer that only moves forward finds j.

explain.intuition:
Since equal damages are compatible, the real choice is per distinct value: take all spells of damage v (worth v · count) or none. Sorted, this is the "house robber" pattern, except that taking a value blocks neighbours within distance 2 by value, not by position in the list.

So for each distinct value, either skip it (keep the best so far) or take it and add the best answer among values strictly below v − 2. Values are sorted, so the last allowed index only moves forward and a second pointer tracks it. A greedy that grabs the biggest value first fails: [7, 9, 9, 10] shows that a single large value can be worth less than a heavy group next to it.
steps: Count each damage value and sort the distinct values v[0] < v[1] < …; let total[i] = v[i] · count.
Let best[i] be the best total using the first i distinct values, with best[0] = 0.
For each i, advance pointer j while v[j] < v[i] − 2; then best[j] covers every compatible smaller value.
pitfalls: Treating each spell separately and forbidding equal damages, which loses the bonus of stacking duplicates.
Looking back only 1 or 2 positions in the distinct list. The forbidden neighbours are defined by value; values 1 and 4 are compatible even when adjacent in the list.
Overflowing a 32-bit integer: the total can reach 10¹⁴.

solutions.title: Try every set of distinct values
solutions.idea: Enumerate subsets of the distinct values, reject those with two values 1 or 2 apart, and take the best sum. Exponential; only for small inputs.

solutions.title: Sorted distinct values with a back pointer
solutions.idea: House robber over distinct values: skip a value, or take all its copies plus the best answer among values below v − 2.

followups: The forbidden distance is a parameter g instead of 2. What changes in the code?
Also return which damage values to cast. How do you reconstruct the choice from the table?
